messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# James

James had been a bus driver for thirty-two years before the men came for him. He was sixty-one now, with a broad chest that had softened slightly with age, hands that knew the weight of a steering wheel through every season, and a reputation among his regular passengers for reliability—the kind of man who showed up, who kept his schedule, who could be counted on. That reputation had meant something to him. It had anchored him through a marriage that had weathered its own turbulence, through the small indignities of municipal employment, through the ordinary erosion of aging in a job that never quite paid what it should.

In 2003, during a humanitarian mission to Central America that he had volunteered for—a two-week stint helping to transport medical supplies to rural clinics—James had been taken from his hotel in a city whose name he had trouble holding in his mind now. The men who came for him had no clear demands. They were looking for American money, or leverage, or simply someone to hurt. What happened over the next four days existed in his memory as a series of fragments: the smell of the room, the specific angle of afternoon light through a high window, the texture of rope against his wrists, the sound of a voice—always that voice—asking questions in Spanish that he did not fully understand, and his own voice, hoarse and pleading, saying things he could not quite remember saying. The pain had been systematic and thorough. He had been waterboarded. He had been beaten. He had been left alone in the dark for hours. He had believed, at certain moments, that he would die there.

He had been released after four days when a local priest had intervened. He had returned to the United States. He had returned to his job. For the first few years, he had told himself it was over—a terrible interlude, something that had happened, something that he had survived. His wife, Maria, had wanted him to see someone, but James had resisted. He was not the kind of man who fell apart. He had gotten through it. He would get through this.

But the getting through had become harder. What James had come to believe, in the quiet hours when he could not sleep, was that he had failed in the most fundamental way. He had been helpless when he should have been strong. He had not fought hard enough, had not resisted with sufficient will, had not protected his own dignity or the dignity of the moment itself. The fact that he was one man against several, that resistance would have been futile, did not touch this conviction. He was certain now that weakness was not something that had happened to him in that room; it was something he was. This belief had seeped into how he understood everything that came after—every moment of fear, every startle response, every night when his body would not let him rest. His weakness explained it all. And because he was weak, because he had failed to be the man he should have been, he remained vulnerable in ways he could not quite articulate but felt with absolute certainty.

That vulnerability had become the texture of his nights. James found it harder to feel safe in darkness than in daylight, and the difference had widened over the years until night had become something he endured rather than experienced. He would lie awake beside Maria, listening for sounds—the creak of a door hinge, a car passing on the street, the neighbor's dog—and each sound would send a spike of adrenaline through his chest. Someone was entering the home. Someone was coming. His body knew this with the certainty of lived knowledge, and no amount of rational reassurance could quiet it. Maria had learned not to move suddenly in bed. She had learned to sleep on the far edge of the mattress, as if distance might help.

When memories surfaced—and they came without warning, triggered by a voice on the radio, the smell of a particular cleaning solution, the sensation of hands gripping his shoulders in a crowd—the terror returned intact, as vivid and overwhelming as if he were still in that room. But the memories themselves were incomplete, fractured. Some moments of the event remained crystalline: the exact pattern of shadows on the wall, the words of a prayer he had whispered, the weight of his own thirst. Other stretches had simply vanished, leaving gaps that his mind could not or would not cross. This fragmentation haunted him. The missing pieces felt like evidence of how badly he had broken, how thoroughly the experience had shattered something essential. And each time he tried to remember, each time a fragment surfaced and brought the terror with it, it reinforced his conviction that he had been fundamentally weak—that a stronger man would have endured differently, would have remembered more clearly, would not be sitting here at sixty-one, unable to sleep in his own bed, listening to the house settle around him as if it were a threat.

The cycle had tightened over the years. His conviction that he was weak, that he had failed, that he could not have done anything differently and yet should have—this belief made every sensation of threat feel more real, more confirming. And every night of vigilance, every startle response, every moment when his body reacted before his mind could catch up, seemed to prove the belief true. He was broken. He was still in danger. The danger was inside him now, and he could not escape it because it was him.

Six months ago, Maria had finally insisted. She had found him one morning on the kitchen floor, having gotten up at three in the morning and simply stayed there, unable to return to bed, unable to move. She had called their primary care physician. The physician had referred him to a trauma specialist. James had resisted for weeks, but Maria had been firm in a way she had not been about many things in their marriage, and James, despite everything, did not want to lose her. He had made an appointment. He had sat in a waiting room full of magazines he did not read, waiting to be called in, wondering if talking about what had happened would make it worse, wondering if a therapist would see what he saw—a weak man who had failed when it mattered most, who deserved the nights he endured, who would never forgive himself for the person he had become.
